The concept of consistent matchings was introduced by Amin and ZEMEL in 2016,
initially for the process of one-to-one matching of eligible students with available school slots. These matchings must adhere to two criteria: first, a student must be matched to a school they consider better than any other; second, co-students at the same institution must also be matched to schools that are equally desirable or better. Based on this framework, we have developed an algorithm called the Consensus Chain model that can efficiently compute optimal solutions for one-to-one student-school matchings under the consistent matching constraint. This algorithm can be adapted for the more general setting of many-to-many student-school matchings, where students can attend one of multiple schools. Our approach involves a reduction of the many-to-many problem into a series of one-to-one student-school matchings. We have also developed a heuristic solution called the Consensus Chain Heuristic that can be run in parallel to yield multiple optimal or near-optimal solutions for both the one-to-one and many-to-many cases.

The development and deployment of complex and diverse computing systems are hindered by the difficulties of integrating and combining various components, such as processors, accelerators, and customized hardware, in a unified system. To address this challenge, a modular approach has been proposed, where individual components, known as "chiplets," can be designed independently and then assembled together onto a single die, known as a "leader chiplet." This approach requires the development of specialized tools to enable seamless communication between chiplets and allow the creation of unified programs that can execute across different components. This document outlines a framework for writing applications that are compatible with these components, known as "Codelets," which can be easily combined and deployed on a variety of systems. It also discusses the key design considerations for developing these components, as well as the potential benefits and limitations of this approach.

A recently introduced model, the mixture cure model, is used to analyze a subset of responses that are classified as non-susceptible. This model is particularly useful in areas such as medical and cancer research where the non-susceptible population needs to be identified. A major challenge associated with this model is estimating the distribution of the latent susceptibility model, which is a parametric component. A novel approach to address this issue is a presmoothing estimation method, as described in the study. This method involves smoothing the incomplete data for the susceptible population using a kernel-based technique. This enables the calculation of complete-likelihood-based estimators for the distribution of the latent susceptibility model. In addition to theoretical proofs, the effectiveness of this method was verified through simulations and a real-world application of its use in pediatric leukemia data analysis.

The nonlocal measure dimension is a metric that measures the coverage of a set by using a nonlocal measure, specifically the packing measure, initially introduced in (Ostrovsky and Pudovskiy 2022) was utilized to analyze the efficiency of error-correcting codes. This paper explores a related concept known as the graph's measure dimension, initially introduced in (Koivisto and Koivisto 2018), which can be applied to any covering measure, including the nonlocal measure, to derive a characterization of the nonlocal measure dimension. Additionally, the paper investigates the computability of the nonlocal measure dimension in graphs and specific instances, such as the computation of nonlocal measure dimension in planar graphs and the computation of nonlocal measure dimension in power graphs.

Emerging in-memory computing (IMC) systems, powered by non-volatile memory (NVM), are being explored for boosting AI processing efficiency. However, the security of these systems is a pressing concern, with this paper investigating the vulnerability of IMC-based AI systems to data manipulation attacks from nearby data channels. We conducted the first comprehensive analysis of these side-channel threats using simulated attacks on various IMC architectures. Our experiments showed that IMC-based systems are particularly susceptible to side-channel threats, with these threats significantly compromising model accuracy even at relatively high levels of noise. The findings suggest that IMC-based systems may require novel security measures to counteract side-channel threats.

We suggest a set of simplified polarization kernels that facilitate the computation of the two-dimensional cross-correlation polarization response function. The polarization response function, which is derived from the Fourier transform of the polarization kernel, serves as a crucial component in determining the polarization spectrum. By employing the method of steepest descent, we have obtained the polarization kernels for commonly encountered time-domain pulse shapes, including Gaussian, rectangular, and triangular functions. The explicit expressions for these reduced polarization kernels are: (i) for Gaussian pulses, $\propto \exp(-\gamma^2)$, where the pre-factor $\gamma$ is inversely proportional to the square root of the pulse width; (ii) for rectangular pulses, $\propto 1/\gamma^3"; where the parameter $\gamma^3$ is inversely proportional to the square root of the pulse width; and (iii) for triangular pulses, $\propto 1/\gamma^3; " with $\gamma^3$ being proportional to the square root of the pulse width. The kernels are most effective when the pulse width is much narrower than the coherence time of the initial state.

Seismic noise, primarily originating from near surface human activities and wind, can severely hinder the detection and analysis of seismic events, causing significant obstacles for automated and manual inspections. Removing seismic interference from data is a critical, however often infeasible, task, given the absence of suitable background data and forward models. This research introduces a data-driven, blind-spot seismic noise reduction technique, utilizing a transfer learning approach. This innovative method is built upon a self-supervised artificial neural network designed to learn seismic wave characteristics from a dataset of non-correlated examples. This trained network is then utilized to remove seismic interference from data from a separate dataset, enabling the identification of seismic events, as demonstrated through the effectiveness of this approach on real-world data from the Trieste seismic network. This research presents a novel approach to automatically decrease background seismic interference in seismic data, enabling the detection and analysis of seismic events, thereby enhancing the efficiency of data interpretation.

The inclusion of charge-asymmetric correlations in elastic lepton- and antilepton-nucleon scattering is investigated through the initial state's real photon emission process in QED.  The interaction is represented in the 16-component formalism incorporating spin, charge, and isospin, and the resulting matrix element is decomposed into these factors.  The resulting expressions yield the asymmetries in terms of the nucleon's isospin components and the transverse components of the lepton and antilepton. A discussion of the physical implications follows, specifically in regards to the application of this method to high-energy particle colliders.

To gain insight into the low-energy spectrum of Sr$_2$IrO$_4$, we employ scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS) and density functional theory (DFT) to analyze the behavior of pure and doped samples. By incorporating the effects of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) on the electronic and magnetic properties of Sr$_2$Ir$_{1-x}$Mg$_x$O$_4$, we investigate the impact of hole doping on the material's electronic structure. The STS spectra of doped samples reveal a significant reduction in the energy of the spin-orbit gap, while the behavior of the spin-orbit gap in the undoped case suggests that it is a quantum critical point. Furthermore, we propose a continuum model to describe the spin-polaron ladder spectrum, which is supported by the STS spectra of Sr$_2$IrO$_4$.

Researchers are increasingly interested in assessing mediation effects, which has driven the development of various mediation analysis techniques. At the same time, the field of causal inference has advanced significantly. Building on this knowledge, we aim to establish a unified framework for causal mediation analysis, incorporating insights from both fields. In this study, we propose a new method for assessing median outcome-specific curves and average treatment effects in mediation scenarios. Our approach builds on the robust estimation principles employed in multiply robust estimators, particularly those developed by local linearization. The local linearization multiple robust (LLMR) method enables us to evaluate different aspects of mediation effects, including direct and indirect effects, natural indirect effects, and average natural indirect effects, as well as total effects, all through a single estimation procedure. Our method is robust to various forms of model misspecification and can be applied in a wide range of contexts, including binary, mixed, and continuous treatments. The results of our simulation studies demonstrate that LLMR outperforms existing techniques in terms of sensitivity to model misspecification. The method has been successfully used in a real-world study examining the impact of a parent-child relationship on anxiety in children.

This Special Issue of the IEEE Transactions on Antennas and Propagation is specifically dedicated to advancements within the realm of optical imaging systems, commonly known as starshades. The technological objective of designing such systems involves enabling the observation of extremely bright sources, which would otherwise be inaccessible with optical detectors. The latest developments within this field have yielded numerous innovative designs and architectures for starshades, primarily employed in the design of large optical systems for space exploration, such as coronagraphs for exoplanetary research, nullifiers for high-powered laser applications, and solar simulators. The issue brings together a comprehensive collection of research papers that highlight the progress of optical imaging systems, with a particular focus on the latest achievements in this field. The papers are accompanied by an introductory section that provides an overview of the field.

A significant number of suicides are likely linked to mental health issues exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, making it crucial to develop a comprehensive understanding of mental wellness strategies that promote well-being. Online mental health resources can offer valuable support, particularly through chatbots and machine learning systems, by providing access to help. However, these technologies can only be effective if they're grounded in a thorough understanding of mental health issues and strategies. This research presents a massive collection of 1.1M annotated online posts expressing various mental health related sentiments, gathered over three years. The dataset has been enriched with additional information, making it the largest publicly available resource of its kind. The research also outlines the collection process and evaluates the effectiveness of text classification models in identifying sentiments, providing valuable insights for machine learning applications. The dataset is now available for public access at \url{https://robinsuicideml.github.io/}.

This paper proposes an extension to Zwartzian mechanics, originally formulated by B. Zwartz in 2016, available in Ref. [1]. The novel development incorporates noncommutative coordinates, analogous to the well-established super Hamiltonian formalism in physics. Utilizing a double noncommutative loop, denoted as $\tau$, allows for the derivation of a modified Lagrangian formulation that incorporates a Darboux coordinate. This new approach is compared to the existing noncommutative Lagrangian formulation of Zwartzian mechanics and a related reformulation using a single noncommutative parameter is presented.

The paper focuses on the analysis of bounded solutions for the given difference equation: $x_{n+1}=ax^\alpha_{n}+bx^\alpha_{n-1}$, where $a, b$ and $\alpha$ are greater than zero. The equation is applicable in medical fields to model cell replication. Initially, the research investigates the conditions for boundedness in the equation when the maximum of $x_n$ is positive and remains constant. The conditions are further divided into two main categories: the first being the boundedness of solutions when the equation is free of the term with $\alpha$ and the second when the equation is influenced by a constant term $c$ that affects its terms. Additionally, the research delves into the conditions for global stability in the equation and the analysis of the unique equilibrium point of the equation. The findings are further demonstrated through an example of the equation $x_{n+1}=ax^{2}_{n}+bx^{2}_{n-1}$, where $a=0.5$, $b=0.4$ and $c=1$, in the medical field to model cell replication.

A collection of s-models based on the Born-Infeld electrodynamics theory is studied in the context of black holes. These models, defined by a specific parameter s, have black holes that behave differently as this parameter changes. Specifically, when s is equal to or greater than 2, the energy density of the black hole solution is upper-bounded, while it remains unbounded when s is less than 2. For s equal to or greater than 2, the magnetic field lines follow a specific pattern, whereas for s less than 2, these lines follow an alternative configuration. Furthermore, when s is less than 2, an additional electric field component is observed. As a result, an analysis of the black hole thermodynamics reveals that its behavior changes as the value of s increases.

An additive $k$-tuple is considered part of the Sidon collection if any subset of $k$ numbers from this tuple results in a unique sum. Similarly, a collection of additive tuples is deemed Sidon if no two tuples produce the same sum when their first entries are paired together in any order. However, a collection of tuples is classified as strongly Sidon if no two tuples themselves can be differentiated based on their initial values. This article explores three strong Sidon conjectures and provides a counterexample to a fourth hypothesis proposed by Hindman and Rosenberg.

The scaling behavior of magnetic susceptibility and geometric phase at finite temperatures has been analyzed within the XY spin series near the critical point. Our investigation, encompassing finite temperature and zero temperature scaling analyses, reveals that the susceptibility exhibits scaling with the exponent γ for any spin value, and the geometric phase's scaling behavior depends on the spin value: it follows the scaling exponent γ/3 when s is odd, and γ/2 when s is even.

Theoretical models of magnetic material behavior, specifically the Ising model, have been extensively used to study various phases, including paramagnetic, ferromagnetic, and spin glass states. Yet, the possibility of a ferromagnetic phase emerging from a non-magnetic one is still not fully understood. In this research, simulations of the Ising model, using a lattice structure, demonstrate that a more energetic paramagnetic state should indeed convert more quickly into a ferromagnetic state. This phenomenon is observed in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional configurations, regardless of the specific interaction potential, as long as it satisfies certain symmetry conditions.

In one-dimensional quasicrystals with power-law hopping, we investigate pairs localization, specifically the tendency of two particles to stay together, using both exact analytical solutions and numerical computations. Our findings indicate that the localization of pairs is significantly influenced by the power-law exponent of hopping and can be either enhanced or suppressed compared to individual particle localization, depending on this exponent. We discovered that the localization of pairs is more stable when the power-law exponent is less than 0.5 than the corresponding individual particle localization, but less so when greater than 1. Furthermore, we observed that the localization of pairs is highly sensitive to these exponents, suggesting that pairs may even become delocalized when the hopping exponent is between 1 and 2. Our numerical computations also reveal the intricate behavior of localization length and delocalization probability as functions of energy and hopping position, as well as a novel phenomenon where the localization of pairs exhibits a re-entrance transition as a function of energy for certain power-law exponents.

The proliferation of digital assistants has led to an increased demand for developing conversational AI systems capable of communicating with users across diverse languages. This research focuses on task-driven conversational systems, which provide specific and concise responses to user queries. We examine the current advancements in Natural Language Processing to support the development of these systems, highlighting the challenges of creating multilingual systems and proposing a comprehensive framework for cross-lingual generalization. This framework encompasses three primary axes: language representation, conversation structure, and system architecture. We illustrate the potential of cross-lingual models by showcasing a multilingual chatbot that can engage in comprehensive, informative conversations in French, German, Japanese, and English. This study aims to inspire the creation of more versatile and adaptable conversational AI systems capable of communicating effectively with users in various languages.

A fundamental mechanism governing how genes code for proteins is alternative splicing, and pre-print studies have shown evidence of dynamic and adaptive splicing in response to environmental stimuli and disease progression. To investigate this phenomenon further, we analyzed short-term changes in differential splicing at a detailed level and discovered that many genes undergo temporary alterations in their expression. We also found evidence that these variations in gene expression are influenced by a gene's inherent properties, including the length of its exons and introns, and its interaction with regulatory elements. Notably, we also identified cases where multiple genes exhibit coordinated changes in gene expression, and we propose that these examples highlight various strategies that genes may use for regulation.

Information technologies are increasingly becoming the focal point of discussions surrounding data privacy regulations, yet the impact of these laws on technical aspects is not always well-understood. To gain a deeper insight into this knowledge gap, a qualitative research study was conducted with IT professionals who are aware of data protection regulations, examining their experiences in implementing technical aspects of these laws within their organizations. By analyzing the responses from 18 participants, it was found that a significant number of technical professionals lack a thorough understanding of data protection regulations, often rely on external expertise, and struggle to navigate the complex technical aspects of these laws. These findings are expected to inform the development of improved educational materials, compliance frameworks, and data protection practices that better engage technical professionals in the compliance process.

We examine the multi-particle azimuthal angular correlations resulting from the interactions between protons and gold nuclei at the collision energy of 660 GeV. Specifically, we focus on the behavior of harmonics, such as $v_2$, $v_3$, etc., in these collisions and their collective characteristics. Using a theoretical model, we establish that these observables can be explained by the interplay between a randomly moving proton and a rotating gold nucleus, where the nucleus's rotational motion is described by a two-dimensional Fourier series. This model allows us to derive analytical expressions for the azimuthal correlations, enabling us to calculate the observed multiparticle distributions. Our findings indicate that the amplitudes of even harmonics in the gold nucleus's Fourier series have a significant impact on the results. We also demonstrate that the shapes of the azimuthal angular correlations can provide valuable information about the rotational properties of the gold nucleus, such as its rotational frequency and angular momentum.

A comprehensive study of light nuclei formation in gold-gold collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 3 GeV was conducted using the STAR detector at RHIC. A broad range of coalescence models was evaluated to understand light nuclei production mechanisms. These models were applied to simulation data generated from a comprehensive event sample, and their parameters were adjusted to achieve optimal agreement with experimental findings. Analysis revealed that different coalescence models can accurately describe data but may over- or underestimate certain multiplicities. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that quark coalescence models can effectively explain light nuclei formation, and suggests that quark-driven coalescence mechanisms are significant in both light and strange nuclei production.

The NASA Architecture Analysis Program's assessment of future space missions
provides valuable input in identifying areas of focus for the community and
setting priorities. A recent review of the program's findings regarding the
search for extraterrestrial life and the study of planetary atmospheres has
highlighted the significance of analyzing the environments of rocky planets.
Recent studies have provided insights into the atmospheric dynamics of exoplanets
which, in turn, are influencing how scientists interpret data from these
planets. To advance our understanding, we must develop tools capable of
analyzing the environments of exoplanets. In this context, we outline a path
focusing on the atmospheres of rocky planets with focus on the detailed dynamics
and composition analysis of these planets.

The process of dispersing a graph involves the product of successive random walks of length $l$, where the result is a new graph with properties derived from independent random steps on the original graph. A graph is said to be dispersible if, given a sufficiently large number $n$ as the size of the graph, the resulting product graph has a diameter that grows proportionally with $l$. This paper establishes the dispersibility of specific graph families, including toroidal circuits and graphs with irregular patterns on multiple prime numbers, and provides bounds on diameter and eigenvalue analysis for graphs with regular patterns on one or two prime factors.

This study expands upon previous research into fast iterative matrix inversion methods, particularly focusing on its application with third-order factors to optimize finite element solutions for non-Newtonian elasto-plastic materials. The proposed approach has been compared to previously developed second-order methods, and its implementation was further adapted for parallel acceleration using the GPU. The findings demonstrate that leveraging third-order factors can significantly enhance the performance of finite element simulations. A comparison of the computational cost and efficiency reveals that using third-order factors can result in a 9.7 times speedup over second-order methods, and a 1.5 times speedup over a purely Newton-based solver. The proposed GPU-accelerated implementation using third-order factors has shown an additional 1.39 times speedup over second-order factors, and 10.33 times overall speedup over the Newton solver.

We examine the power spectrum of primordial fluctuations in ultra-low speed inflation scenarios, incorporating the impact of quantum fluctuations into both the tensor and scalar spectra. This analysis reveals that the power spectrum of tensor fluctuations exhibits a linear relationship with the inflationary scale, whereas the power spectrum of scalar fluctuations displays a distinct change in slope at a specific scale, different from the pivot scale, and this change occurs regardless of the number of e-folds. By comparing our findings with recent research on ultra-low speed inflation with quantum fluctuations and back reaction effects, we demonstrate that our results hold considerable potential for improving inflationary model analysis.

In online retail, where digital products prevail, there is an increasing demand for personalized recommendations tailored to individual customers' preferences, rather than offering a fixed set of products to all. To effectively cater to each customer's needs, retailers can adopt an online algorithm that continuously updates the available product selection based on customer feedback. This online process is referred to as online assortment optimization, and the problem we're focusing on is known as the enhanced assortment optimization, where the goal is to select a limited number of products from a large, predefined set to maximize the expected revenue. Each customer's utility for the selected products is calculated by a linear function, dependent on a randomly generated parameter, and the optimal selection is made without any prior knowledge of the customers' specific preferences. This online variant of the enhanced assortment optimization problem is particularly relevant in digital retail, where the customers' tastes keep changing due to the dynamic nature of the online environment.

The case-based case series design is widely applied in medical and biomedical research but lacks a standardized analysis method. As a result, the design's potential is not fully realized. This study aims to develop and propose a set of statistical techniques for analyzing case-based case series data to facilitate the design's widespread adoption. The suggested analysis approach is comprehensive, flexible, and tailored to discrete time-to-event outcomes. For continuous-time survival data, the analysis can be implemented by treating the events as discrete, allowing for the estimation of various parameters, including mean and quantiles. The analysis is validated through simulations under different scenarios. The proposed framework is then demonstrated using a dataset from a pilot trial examining the effect of a new compound on patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Future high-precision measurements in particle physics will require advanced methods to compute mathematical integrals over multiple variables. To achieve this, we are developing tools to analytically integrate Feynman integrals with up to five points (amplitudes) and variables. Our project's primary objective is to create a general algorithm to integrate arbitrary Feynman integrals with both scalar and vector integrands. Building on existing algorithms, we will integrate integrals with up to five points and variables using existing algorithms. To ensure the accuracy and stability of our methods, we will employ existing algorithms, such as multi-scale integration and fitting techniques, to create a general algorithm. To validate our methods, we will apply them to existing integrals and create new ones, with the goal of creating a library of mathematical integrals to support future precision physics experiments.

The performance of the Lustre system was compared to DAOS for managing object data. Lustre was found to be more suitable for serving object-based files but processing tasks were slower due to high overhead. In contrast, the new Lustre Client Library 2.0 allowed for object data to be processed directly, reducing the need for copying data. Performance metrics including benchmark results from Pinball, MPI benchmark, and the SLURM workload manager were collected for single-node and multi-node configurations. Findings indicated that using the Lustre Client Library 2.0 could increase performance by 2-3x for object-based file I/O and by 1.5x for MPI communication. Meanwhile, the SLURM benchmark revealed a consistent performance with both DAOS and Lustre for various task types.

A new digital system, ePark, has been developed to address the growing need for efficient parking management in smart cities. This particpants for permission to access parked and charged vehicles can be sent to owners via mobile apps, using a unique access code generated by parking meters, allowing users to authorize designated individuals to retrieve vehicles or collect payment in real-time. A cloud-based ePark platform has been proposed to manage and allocate access codes to users, utilizing an ePark cloud service to support various smart parking applications. This proposed system has been evaluated through simulations, demonstrating its feasibility in practical settings.

This study delves into the theory of linear code (LC) and linear complementary dual code (LCD), particularly focusing on creating such codes over a finite field using specific combinatorial techniques and an extension of the Zeros-Intersection approach for non-binary values. The work also investigates the properties of these codes and their duals, and provides concrete examples and an in-depth case study to demonstrate its findings.

The EFT'ALE' framework enables us to derive conventional gravity's action from amplitudes through the EFT'ALE' formula, which involves the product of loop amplitudes and their respective cuts, scaled by an exponential factor that depends on external momenta. This exponential factor's behavior as momentum tends towards infinity indicates that the EFT'ALE' formula is only valid for relatively low-energy regimes. We investigate the behavior of EFT'ALE' amplitudes in the presence of a single external graviton and demonstrate that, in the infrared limit, these amplitudes yield soft-collinear expansion, which is consistent with the conventional soft graviton theorem. We also observe that, at tree level, EFT'ALE' amplitudes exhibit local gauge invariance. However, loop corrections to these amplitudes introduce potential issues, which we address by examining the one-loop corrections to three-point amplitudes. We find that, to correct for these problems, one must include the one-loop corrections to the exponential factor in the EFT'ALE' formula.

A massive shift towards solar energy is anticipated in the Western United States, prompting concerns about land degradation and energy production trade-offs. We developed a policy map for the region's first tier states, analyzing various land-based alternatives to identify optimal locations and energy output distributions. We created a decarbonization strategy for the region, exploring the implications of transitioning away from fossil fuels and assessing the land requirements necessary to replace current power plants with new solar facilities. We discovered that solar production could be significantly increased with minimal land-based switching between alternative energy sources, and that the initial phase-out of fossil fuels would result in considerable energy output redistribution.

Cluster randomized trials are frequently employed to evaluate vaccines by assigning entire groups, such as healthcare facilities or neighborhoods, to treatment arms, often using open-label dosing. Estimating the efficacy of vaccines within these trials poses a significant challenge, particularly when there's a mismatch between the assigned unit of analysis and the one of primary interest. To address this, we examine existing methods for estimating the causal effect of individual participation in vaccination, particularly when only cluster-level data are available and not individual records. Our analysis reveals instances where conventional analyses can provide valid estimates of the target parameters but are often subject to substantial bias. Conversely, traditional analyses of clustered data can yield misleading results. To address this, we propose two valid methods for determining the causal effect of individual participation: one that utilizes cluster-level covariates and another based on individual data. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of the latter method in overcoming confounding biases by utilizing individual covariates in finite samples.

We introduce a novel fractal family, the M\"{o}bius octagonal network, which emerges from repeatedly applying specific transformations to a basic octagonal shape with alternating symmetry. This new family extends the analysis of M\"{o}bius networks, which have been explored in various contexts, to include a combination of octagonal and ring configurations. The goal of this research is to systematically study the spectral characteristics of the M\"{o}bius octagonal network, with a focus on its degree distribution and normalized Laplacian spectrum. The investigation also considers the spectral and connectivity properties of the M\"{o}bius octagonal network, with potential applications in transport properties, network synchronization, graph theory, and physics, which will be explored further in this presentation.

In a distributed contextual online learning framework, a group of agents collaborate to minimize their combined regret by using linear bandits in a multi-arm setting with the "Linear Bandit with Linear Rewards" model. Each agent receives the same context but has separate reward functions. With no requirement of shared variables, arms, or communication overhead, a new distributed algorithm called D-UCRL is developed and analyzed. It achieves an expected cumulative regret of $\tilde{O}( \sqrt{B C} \sqrt{K} )$ after $K$ rounds, where $B$ is the maximum conditional mean reward, $C$ is the maximum noise variance of rewards, and $K$ is the total rounds. This result is the first distributed linear bandit algorithm that does not require shared variables and only achieves a $\tilde{O}( K \sqrt{B C} )$ bound in the best case. Additionally, a more efficient distributed bandit algorithm is developed for a specific scenario where the context, arm space, and variables are shared. It achieves a $ \tilde{O}( B \sqrt{C K} ) $ regret in the best case scenario. This result is also the first to do so in the specific case of the "Linear Bandit with Linear Reward" model.

Supplementing clinical data analysis tools with synthetic health records can be beneficial, enabling the evaluation of new treatments and disease progression models. To create a cohort of electronic health records for Cystic Fibrosis patients, we developed a synthetic data generator using a time-series model for visit records and a model for laboratory results. This generator was evaluated by comparing its output to real patient records using two metrics - a clinical reviewer's assessment of generated records, and a measure of statistical differences between synthetic and real records. The results show that synthetic records closely matched real records in both clinical and statistical evaluations.

The $D^{0} \to K^\mp \pi^\pm \pi^\mp \pi^\mp$ decays are examined using $pp$ collision data collected at $\sqrt{s} = 7$ and $8\,\mathrm{TeV}$ by the LHCb experiment, which collects a total integrated luminosity of $3.0\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$. A novel approach is utilized to account for the $\pi^-\pi^+$ mass distribution complexity, which is divided into groups of resonances that are modelled within an unbinned extended maximum-likelihood fit. A novel $D^{0} \to K^0_S \pi^+\pi^-\pi^+$ decay mode is observed, which is determined to have a branching fraction of $(3.72 \pm 0.65 \pm 0.17 \pm 0.45 \pm 0.45) \times 10^{-3}$, with the first uncertainty attributed to fitting, the second to normalisation, the third to the $D^{0} \to K^0_S K^\pm \pi^\mp$ branching fraction and fourth to the treatment of the phase space.

Bibliometric data and patent information often provide valuable insights into an individual's contributions to their field, the direction of scientific progress, and the significance of published research.  Despite various methods for assessing the impact of scientific publications, there is a lack of standard approaches for evaluating the freshness of bibliometric data and its potential to revolutionize an associated domain, addressed by the 'Novelpy' Python package.  'Novelpy' calculates two key metrics: (i) the 'Novelty Index' to gauge the innovation factor of an individual's publications relative to their total, and (ii) the 'Disruptiveness Density' to measure the potential to revolutionize a domain's knowledge structure; both metrics are grounded in knowledge graph theory and employ a novel 'Domain Index' to enable the evaluation of an individual's influence on an existing domain.  'Novelpy' provides a user-friendly interface for constructing a knowledge graph and calculating the 'Novelty Index' and 'Disruptiveness Density'.  'Novelpy' has been applied in an empirical study to examine the scientific careers of women and men across various stages of their careers, and its effectiveness in capturing the dynamics of field evolution and influence on an individual's contributions to their field, and their overall impact, is demonstrated.

A single laser beam with non-uniform intensity can be manipulated in space and time through the interaction of multiple correlated beams. To achieve this, a method is developed for creating a set of partially coherent waves with identical spectral profiles. These waves are then passed through a medium at different points, and due to cross-phase modulation, they interact and modulate each other's intensity. As a result, the combined beam exhibits spatial and temporal patterns of self-adjusting intensity as the initial waves interfere and evolve over time. The mechanism behind this intensity regulation is demonstrated through both numerical simulations and experiments. The study also examines the impact of partial coherence on the efficiency and regulation of self-adjusting intensity, and it is shown that the spatial and temporal patterns of the modulated intensity can be controlled using a single laser beam.

This study investigates the technical feasibility of equipping a robotic arm with a bow for archery, specifically the Olympic recurve, and its motorized components. We analyze the key characteristics of the system, identify potential technical challenges, and propose a solution to mitigate the issues that arise from the bow's flexible properties and the robotic system. The paper also outlines a specifically designed robotic configuration to perform the task.

Cross-domain recommendation systems have become increasingly popular, enabling users to find relevant items based on their preferences, even when their preferences are associated with specific devices, contexts, or scenarios. However, most cross-domain approaches are either inefficient due to their reliance on computationally expensive operations or ineffective as they only learn a single representation that might not capture the unique characteristics of each domain. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel cross-domain recommendation model that employs a novel dual metric learning approach. This approach learns two independent representations, one tailored to each domain, by modeling the relationships between items and users within each domain. Furthermore, we develop a dual metric learning objective that enables the model to preserve meaningful differences between items and users across different domains. We also introduce a new training strategy that allows the model to learn from multiple source domains efficiently. Experimental evaluations conducted on cross-device recommendation and personalized speaker recommendation datasets demonstrate that our model surpasses state-of-the-art models in both effectiveness and efficiency.

The modal mu-calculus is a widely recognized logic that precisely expresses properties of pointed labeled trees. Within the scope of distributed computing, the modal mu-calculus serves as a precise language for describing behaviors within asynchronous systems. Consequently, determining whether a modal mu-expression is definable in this context, known as being within the modal mu-characteristic fragment (MCH), is a significant question. Prior research demonstrated that the problem of whether an expression is MCH is definable is undecidable in general. This paper presents a groundbreaking outcome by establishing a decision-making algorithm for this question within linear modal mu-calculus, a variant of the original that is equivalent to the characteristic fragment. This breakthrough is achieved by redefining the concept of characteristic fragment in relation to the linear modal mu-calculus, and in turn, simplifying the analysis through the use of an innovative characterization of definable expressions within linear modal mu, which is based on a novel concept of modal mu-expressions that are definable within a specific machine-based framework.

Researchers have been studying the temperature exchange processes within two-dimensional complex plasmas contained in the Birkhoff fluid model.  The primary goal of the study is to examine how temperature exchange varies in response to changes in the ratio of inter-particle to inter-layer distances, specifically $d^*$.  This investigation revealed that heat transfer in 2D complex plasmas can be limited, resulting in temperature gradients emerging along the vertical axis, rather than horizontally.  Furthermore, it was discovered that the vertical temperature difference ($\Delta T_{vert}$) is influenced by $d^*$, with the ratio being inversely proportional.  A relationship between $\Delta T_{vert}$ and $d^*$ was also established, showing a direct linear correlation.  However, it was found that when $d^*$ exceeds a certain threshold ($d^*>1$), heat transfer becomes limited, leading to horizontal temperature uniformity.  This study has also led to the development of a simple equation describing the horizontal temperature profile, as well as the relationship between the vertical temperature difference and $d^*$.

We examine the variety of linear combinations of unordered data sets, characterizing them through a finite, algebraic system derived from the combination rules. Furthermore, we investigate the basic properties of these linear combinations, demonstrating that any unordered data vector can be expressed as a linear combination of three fundamental elements. Additionally, we analyze the relationship between such linear combinations and permutation-equivalence, establishing that the equivalence class of unordered data vectors defined by linear combinations is a finite, algebraic system.

Cardiac fluoroscopy is a crucial tool for interventional cardiology, but it poses a problem due to the high X-ray radiation levels that increase the risk of cancer and small vessel disease. To address this issue, we investigated the potential of deep learning-based video interpolation (DL4VI) to reduce radiation levels during procedures. Our study involved analyzing real-world data from cardiac fluoroscopy, where we compared the use of DL4VI with the standard approach, finding a significant decrease in average dose radiation during experiments. The new approach also maintained image quality, as assessed by both human evaluation and objective metrics. The potential implications of this innovation are significant, leading to improved clinical outcomes and lower healthcare costs.

We examine the potential of heavy-flavor physics in the FCC-ee program using real photons and photon-factories. After discussing the principles behind heavy-flavor production through photons, we focus on two key areas of heavy-flavor production: the production of charmed and beauty particles, and heavy-quarkonium production. We then explore the proposed experimental setups, including the use of real photons and photon-factories to detect these particles, and identify the challenges associated with experimental measurements and analyze the expected precision in extracting key parameters such as the $b$ quark mass and the decay constants of charmed and beauty B mesons.

The investigation of muon and tau lepton numbers in relation to dark matter is a significant area of research.  The connection between dark matter and charged fermions is a crucial aspect, with a specific charge assignment for $L_{\mu}$ and $L_{\tau}$ being a common choice.  This paper examines the impact of this assignment on the neutrinoless double beta decay and dark matter direct detection, leveraging the existing knowledge of $U(1)_{L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}}$ models.  The findings suggest that a specific dark matter direct detection experiment can test a substantial portion of parameter space, even in the most favorable scenarios.  The analysis reveals that a dark matter direct detection experiment with a certain sensitivity can test a significant portion of parameter space, even in the most favorable scenarios.

We investigate the potential origin of high-speed stars originating from the Milky Way's core through a massive intermediate-mass companion star. By simulating the long-term impact of this star's gravitational influence, we analyze the escape routes of stars from the star cluster at the Galaxy's center. The results indicate that the outer regions of star clusters are likely to lose stars with velocities exceeding 500 to 1000 km/s, with an estimated 0.035 to 0.72 percent of stars escaping as high-speed velocities. The formation of these high-speed stars is contingent upon the companion star's mass, ranging from 0.2 to 10 solar masses, and their orbit's eccentricity, particularly their proximity to the point of maximum eccentricity, at a distance of approximately 0.05 to 0.1 au. The high-speed stars are likely to be the remnants of stars that were once bound to the star cluster. The presence of these high-speed stars as well as those found in the hypervelocity category may be attributed to the same intermediate-mass companion star.

In this work, we establish the existence of weak solutions for a class of singular multiplicative stochastic differential equations. Our approach builds on previous research by Rozkosz and \v{S}ili\'nski, yet we diverge from their method, which examines strong solutions, to instead analyze the existence of weak solutions for equations featuring a singular stochastic integral. By employing a noise perturbation technique, we demonstrate the existence of weak solutions for these equations under mild conditions, including the condition of integrability of drift coefficients and high volatility, as well as the condition of non-integrability of volatility with respect to Lebesgue measure.

Under large cardinal conditions, we examine the essential properties of the nonstationary ideal on $\omega_1$ and its corresponding $P(\omega_1)$ model.  Specifically, we investigate its basic measures, $S$, $S[X]$ and $R(X)$, as well as its stationary subset's behavior.  It is demonstrated that the uniqueness of the basic measures under certain forcing conditions leads to the $\Delta^<_{\omega}_n$-definability of the NSH property, thereby yielding an alternative proof of a prior result by Friedman and Cummings.  Additionally, we explore the impact of certain forcing conditions on the $\Delta^<_\kappa$-definability of the NSH property.

Significant advancements have been made in natural language understanding in recent
years, but recent breakthroughs have been hindered by the challenge of adapting
general-purpose language models to the nuances of a specific domain or task.
To address this, we introduce Adaptor - a comprehensive framework for creating
domain- and task-specific language models. Adaptor empowers the creation of
customized models for diverse applications such as information retrieval and
visual content description. We demonstrate that Adaptor facilitates domain- and
task-aware training, fine-tuning, and inference, and that models developed via
Adaptor surpass state-of-the-art performance on datasets in 7 different domains
and 12 diverse tasks.

A new dataset focusing on global traffic signals is presented, featuring over
1.3 million annotated traffic signals from around the world, enabling the
development of a more comprehensive traffic signal detection and classification
system across different locations and regions. This dataset, compiled from
Mapillary's vast crowd-sourced data, is now fully available for use.

Recent advances in self-supervised learning have led to several novel methods for collaborative filtering, but they often require significant modifications to traditional CF models, leading to complex architectures and challenging optimization problems. In response, we introduce SelfCF, a flexible and widely applicable framework that can be seamlessly integrated with traditional CF models, leveraging a single cross-view contrastive loss to learn meaningful representations. Surprisingly, even this simple approach has proven highly effective on a range of real-world datasets, surpassing the performance of various state-of-the-art methods and boasting improved computational efficiency.

We establish that the canonically defined Tevelev levels of $\mathbbP^1$ (which were originally introduced in \cite{Tevelev} in the broader context of general smooth spaces) can be determined through a straightforward, algebraic criterion.

A Dirac semimetal with both linear and quadratic dispersion bands coexisting is examined.  The interaction between these bands generates an inherent gap in the system's topological structure.  The study reveals that this system has no quantum spin Hall effect when it's at half-filling.  However, if electrons occupy one band and holes occupy the other, a quantum spin Hall insulator emerges provided the system has sufficient spin-orbit coupling.  The system's topological properties can be visualized using a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological index, which also applies to more complex cases with multiple bands of linear and quadratic dispersions.

We examine the long-term behavior of a slow, stable curve in the vicinity of an isolated holomorphic curve, specifically how it enters and exits the surrounding holomorphic curve field. Our analysis reveals that, generically, this behavior is characterized by a simple recurrent sequence with a periodic focus of length two. We have proven a key theorem for the case when the curve is not isolated and its neighboring curve is one-dimensional, establishing the existence of a recurrent trajectory with a period of two when the zero is the only accumulation point of the curve's parameters. Our theorem is an extension of a previous result by Birkhoff for isolated holomorphic curves, and it provides a more accurate representation of non-generic situations. We have also explored the case of a non-generic curve with a periodic focus of a different length, but with a more complex characteristic.

Future third-generation gravitational-wave detectors are expected to have improved sensitivity, with significant boosts in strain detection, allowing them to detect sources that were previously undetectable. This paper explores the detection capabilities of these advanced detectors for complex waveforms containing gravitational waves and fluid oscillations. By combining analytical and numerical approaches, we identified parameters that enable the detection of elevated mode patterns in specific types of binary black hole signals, including those with higher spins and increased mass. We also examined the effects of varying source distances, detector sensitivity, and computational tools on elevated mode detectability, ultimately establishing a set of criteria for third-generation detector observations that could reveal new features of these astrophysical phenomena.

Astronomers have long been fascinated by the behavior of binary stars, particularly when one star orbits the other, causing it to periodically darken. By modeling these changing shadows, researchers can gain valuable insights into the stars' masses and orbital arrangements, leading to a better understanding of how binary systems evolve over time. Using Gaia's astrometric data, scientists have been able to study the orbits of close binary stars, even when follow-up spectroscopy is not available. Gaia's early data release revealed that the instrument's ability to track the orbits of these stars is limited to a certain point, beyond which the binary stars appear as a single entity on Gaia's sky. By combining these observations with data from the Kepler mission, we have created a new method, called $d$-shadow, that can utilize Gaia's data to measure the orbits of binary stars, even when only a portion of their orbit is visible. Our method has been successfully tested on 1,000 simulated binary stars, resulting in accurate orbital parameter measurements for nearly 70% of them, even when their full orbits are not visible. By applying this method to a sample of 1,000 genuine binary stars, we have found that the $d$-shadow method is capable of measuring the orbits of approximately 30% of them, even when their full orbits are not visible. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of genetic algorithms in solving the 0/1 Knapsack problem, with a focus on the performance of various selection and crossover methods. To this end, three genetic algorithms were developed, each employing a unique selection method: stochastic selection, tournament selection, and truncation selection. Furthermore, the genetic algorithms were tested with distinct single crossover, multiple crossover, and random crossover techniques. The results revealed that a genetic algorithm that combines truncation selection and random crossover achieved the fastest convergence, yielding optimal solutions for the majority of tested instances within a reasonable time frame.

This paper presents $L^2$ estimates, specifically the $L^2-L^2-L^2$ estimate, for trilinear convolution operators that translate specific types of oscillatory estimates from functions to convolution kernels. Initially, we apply this $L^2$ estimate to derive the $L^2-L^2-L^2$ estimate for the Airy and Prandtl-Myers operators, and subsequently for the fast oscillating Airy operator.

This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of the T5 model on hate speech detection tasks. We conducted experiments across seven hate speech datasets, examining both HATEXpression and Jigsaw categories, and analyzed the model's performance using various metrics, including macro F1, AUC, and Spacy metrics. In addition, we assessed the model's ability to identify hate words, perform zero-shot and few-shot tasks, and explored the contributions of three datasets to our ensemble model. We also developed a dynamic thresholding approach to enhance the ensemble model's output. Notably, our model achieved top scores on two datasets and produced competitive results on the remaining five datasets.

To investigate the feasibility of achieving interaction scaling in quantum Monte Carlo calculations for heavier ions, we analyze the computational scaling in a simulation of the water molecule, using a simplified model based on the valence electrons of the neon and calcium ions as a system of seven interacting particles. By employing various Monte Carlo algorithms, we evaluate the scaling of the fixed-node ground-state energy with the number of nodes, observing that the multilevel and parallel bandedge algorithms exhibit better convergence with the number of nodes than the diffusion Monte Carlo algorithm. Furthermore, we investigate the critical node count for these algorithms and demonstrate how it correlates with the bandedge matrix and node distribution, specifically noting that the parallel bandedge algorithm can handle up to 1 billion nodes due to its reduced bandedge width. The interaction scaling study reveals that the ground-state energy of the neon-ion-water complex converges rapidly with the neon ion's charge for up to eight nodes per ion.

The 2020 US Presidential Election saw an unprecedented surge in claims of election deception, with many of these false claims spreading through social media. Despite the potential for these misleading statements to influence the election's outcome, there has been a lack of research on the issue or data focused on it. To address this knowledge gap, we've compiled a dataset of election deception claims on Twitter. This multi-modal dataset includes claims of election deception in two formats: text and images. To determine the veracity of these claims, we've used a variety of sources, including fact-checking websites and government sources, to verify the accuracy of these claims. Our analysis of this data has allowed us to identify patterns in how false and true claims differ and to develop methods to identify and assess the impact of these misleading statements on social media platforms. Our findings suggest that false claims are more prevalent and tend to attract more engagement than true claims. Additionally, we've found that the use of images can make misleading statements more convincing. Our work on this data has also allowed us to develop a system for automatically identifying and flagging misleading statements on Twitter.

We examine the behavior of generic hyperbolic diffeomorphisms on compact manifolds with a focus on their nonuniformly hyperbolic characteristics. These diffeomorphisms exhibit continuous density properties and have positive Lyapunov exponents everywhere, but specific examples exist with zero or negative Lyapunov indicators for some diffeomorphism orbits. Under the assumption that the diffeomorphism's derivative has positive determinant everywhere, we show that the diffeomorphism possesses an open set of local diffeomorphisms with non-singular derivative, each of which is an area-expanding homeomorphism. This emergence property allows for the creation of sequences of local diffeomorphisms with non-singular derivative, leading to the construction of sequences of quasi-local diffeomorphisms with non-singular derivative, demonstrating the Zegarlai emergence phenomenon even in the non-uniformly hyperbolic setting.

We present a method to represent the posterior distribution of a Bayesian neural network's output, enabling more effective uncertainty propagation and evaluation. By generating a set of samples from the posterior predictive distribution, our approach outperforms existing techniques in capturing the true uncertainty of a model's output, as verified through various uncertainty measures and assessments. A unique aspect of our approach is its scalability, enabling it to determine the required number of samples automatically and eliminate the need for a control input, which can be a significant advantage in resource-constrained environments.

We have developed a method to analyze the rapid electronic processes that precede the slow, thermally-driven reactions in complex molecular systems, as described by the Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory. This approach is based on a quantum mechanical model that treats the system's electronic component and its nuclear configuration as separate entities. By applying a technique that connects the quantum mechanical model to a simplified, semiclassical model, we are able to study the behavior of the system in a more manageable way, even when the number of its components is extremely large. Through this simplified approach, we have been able to derive the key predictions of the Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory in a more intuitive and accessible manner.

This research introduces a unique trajectory planning method, tailored specifically for implementation within model predictive control frameworks, capable of accurately representing real-world system dynamics. Conventional trajectory planning methods often fail to capture the intricacies of system dynamics due to restrictive assumptions, leading to poor results when integrated with model predictive control. To address this, the paper delves into the underlying causes of these inaccuracies and presents a novel strategy to enhance both the accuracy of trajectory data and the compatibility with model predictive control. This strategy is illustrated through simulations of a quadrotor simulation within the OpenAI Gym environment.

A theoretical framework for the vast thermoelectric effect has been developed based on the magnon drag mechanism. This framework is capable of capturing the complex characteristics of power generation and associated heat currents. By utilizing this model, the thermoelectric properties of a thin-film Heusler alloy, Mn$_2$Yuc$_5$, were calculated and found to exceed the standards set by the thermodynamic scale. This was achieved through the observation of a significant thermopower response in Nernst and Seebeck coefficients. Notably, the Nernst coefficient demonstrated a notable increase, peaking at 10 mV/K, while the Seebeck coefficient showed a significant 800 microV/K/deg variation. This framework is expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of the magnon drag mechanism and provide valuable insights into the control of thermoelectric responses in related materials.

The Perfect Sum problem in Combinatorics involves finding a method to combine constant-length subsets of a given set of positive integers to equal a specified target sum, where the subsets have a predetermined maximum size. This problem has been researched by multiple scientists, particularly through the use of a Boolean Algebra approach by Albert and Wilf [1994], and an integer programming method by Fonda et al. [2014]. This paper instead employs a probabilistic approach, which provides a straightforward method to achieve the target sum with a high likelihood, outperforming previous methods in terms of time complexity. To illustrate its efficacy, the article applies the probabilistic approach to achieve a target sum with subsets of size three from the set {1, 2, 3, 4}, achieving a high probability of success.

In the class of finite fields with defining polynomials of the form $t^q+t^{a}+m$ over $t$, where $a$ is an odd integer and $m$ is a nonzero constant, we investigate elements of elevated order through their minimal polynomials and degree relationships, ultimately deriving a formula to calculate their degree based on field and polynomial parameters.

In our paper, we explore how the model checking framework can be applied to source code analysis, specifically leveraging the UPPAAL tool for system code verification. By mapping programming concepts to timed automata features, we illustrate how key programming elements translate to specific UPPAAL automata properties. We then demonstrate how these translations enable the use of UPPAAL for tasks such as identifying deadlocks, reachability issues, and verifying program properties. To illustrate our methods, we analyze a variety of programming concepts within both C and ASP languages.

Recent research has demonstrated the feasibility of using radio frequency meta surfaces to improve the resolution in radio imaging without increasing the signal bandwidth. This achievement is made possible by the ability of meta surface arrays to adjust their phase response, effectively introducing a spatial sampling function. Building upon this concept, we present an end-to-end enhancement method that leverages compressed sensing to improve the performance of existing meta surfaces without requiring any physical modifications. Our approach is capable of enhancing the performance of meta surfaces that have previously been optimized for maximum gain rather than imaging quality. Furthermore, we show that using our optimization method allows for the reduction of the number of elements in the array, leading to increased flexibility in the design of meta surfaces and reduced manufacturing costs.

Utilizing the Kramers-Henneberger potential in our theoretical framework, we investigate how the shift in the photoionization potential of hydrogen is influenced by the interaction of two highly intense, bichromatic laser fields with orthogonal polarizations. Specifically, we examine the effect on the 1s to nP transition, where n can range from 2 to 6. By calculating the associated transition amplitudes, we derive the corresponding transition amplitudes and probabilities. The results indicate that the shift in the photoionization potential is notably more pronounced when the frequencies of the two laser fields are close to the resonant ionization frequency of hydrogen, with significant discrepancies from the shifts predicted by the average field theory.

We introduce an innovative method for combining two images by exchanging their underlying semantic details. The approach exchanges hidden, semantically meaningful layers between images as opposed to overwriting entire features at once, similar to how filter-based image editing software works. The method yields a new image that retains the original organization and visual details of the initial images while incorporating the shared semantic elements. We propose a semantically meaningful image blending algorithm that identifies and trades similar features between images to produce a new image. The approach also enables a new type of image blending known as "mixed image editing," where multiple images can be combined into a new image that retains all its underlying details. We demonstrate the practical applications of our method through various examples, including mixing facial images, separating objects from backgrounds, and combining multiple semantic segments.

The expression of genes in cells is often represented as a series of random events over time, with each "burst" having a different duration and intensity. To better understand this process, we're analyzing stochastic trajectories of noisy experimental data to extract meaningful features. Our approach uses a combination of techniques, including peak detection, calculation of peak properties, and interval estimation, to analyze these trajectories. These methods are applied to two distinct datasets, one related to the Arabidopsis thaliana circadian clock and the other examining the cell-fate decision-making process in Caenorhabditis elegans.

A significant amount of data is required to train complex machine learning models effectively, but the availability of labeled data is limited compared to unlabeled data. This paper introduces a novel semi-supervised learning approach that utilizes unlabeled data to improve a model's performance. Unlike traditional methods, which rely on generating data like Generative Adversarial Networks, our method transforms the unlabeled data into synthetic labeled data for training. This is achieved by using a neural network to learn the data's transformation and applying it to the unlabeled data. We also propose a loss function to optimize the transformation and ensure the learned function is reliable. Our results show that this method outperforms other semi-supervised learning approaches, including the traditional method based on GANs, when the labeled data are scarce.

The success of Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQE) and Variational Quantum Circuits in the noisy-intermediate-scale quantum era is largely attributed to the optimisation techniques used to prepare initial states.  A novel approach to this problem is proposed, which employs a circuit architecture of alternating layers of unitary operators and parameterised gates.  This method, called Quantum Substitution Optimisation (QSO), allows the training process to build on previously optimised states.  A detailed analysis shows that, similar to deep neural networks, QSO benefit from scaling up their depth.  A thorough experimental evaluation in different scenarios reveals that QSO surpasses other optimisation methods, such as QAOA and Shallow QAO, and approaches state-of-the-art alternatives like QLSO and full-circuit VQE.  Furthermore, the results demonstrate that QSO can effectively leverage larger training sets, and that its performance is less affected by the quality of the initial state.  The experiments also show that QSO can be efficiently parallelised, making it suitable for near-future quantum computing hardware.

We are tackling the complex challenge of identifying individuals within datasets, particularly medical records, while considering the sensitive nature of the information involved. Recent research has made significant strides in this field, but existing methods have been largely theoretical, assuming minimal overlap between datasets, which is far from realistic. In this research, we explore the practicality of secure data sharing and processing, taking into account real-world scenarios where datasets may contain extensive overlap. To this end, we introduce the concept of n-protocol for reliable individual re-identification, which ensures that given access to a dataset, an adversary can identify individuals in at most n records. Furthermore, we examine the efficiency of various implementations of this protocol and provide insights into the lower limits of secure data processing.

To study the behavior of modern power systems accurately, time series data of their behavior is often lacking, prompting the need for synthetic models to fill the gap. Creating these models can be challenging, especially when real-world data is unavailable, as is often the case. Consequently, modern power system researchers frequently rely on historical data sets that are insufficient for their specific needs. To address this issue, this study develops a novel approach to generating realistic time series data using a machine learning technique that preserves the underlying patterns of the original data. The proposed method is then tested on a widely used dataset to evaluate its effectiveness. The results demonstrate that the approach can successfully reconstruct the original time series while maintaining its essential properties, allowing for the generation of multiple scenarios with distinct characteristics. The proposed method is particularly useful for power systems research as it enables the creation of new data sets that can be used to answer specific research questions that cannot be tackled with historical data sets.

We examine a perturbed algorithm, which combines the proximal point method with additional adjustments that alter its iterations exponentially over time. Our analysis demonstrates robust convergence to the sole solution of a variational inequality problem, with this result being achieved under minimal requirements, specifically assuming that the operator within the problem adheres to either Lipschitz or monotone criteria. This outcome surpasses the existing convergence standards for the proximal point method.

Following the guidance of Cross, we examine the structure of sign patterns in hyperbolic triangles formed by geodesic crossings, with a focus on groups classified by Lubotzky-Mozes-Schlichter as being isoxial within their maximal irreducible quotient.  Cross's findings suggest that, for each such group, the sign pattern in its sign pattern matrix exhibits a strong periodicity when viewed through its action via the Schrieber-Mozes representation. We demonstrate that this periodicity can be interpreted as the effect of traversing the fundamental geodesic cycle of the hyperbolic triangle.

The first search for lepton flavor violation in the process of $\Upsilon(3S) \rightarrow e^\pm \mu^{\mp}$ is conducted using $1.1\times10^8$ $\Upsilon(3S)$ events collected by the BESIII detector at the BEPCII collider. Utilizing a time-difference method to minimize background, the results indicate that the upper limit of the process's branching ratio is $1.90\times10^{-6}$ with a statistical significance of $0.16$. This outcome is consistent with the standard model's prediction, indicating that the process's effective coupling does not exceed $0.38$ times the standard model's value.

We investigated the occurrence of superconductivity in the non-magnetic flat-band material Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$ as a function of hydrostatic pressure. Our research revealed that the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) of this compound increases with pressure, reaching a maximum value of 3.0 K at approximately 4.5 GPa, after which it decreases. Our theoretical analysis utilized the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations to understand how a change in the electron-phonon coupling constant ($\lambda$) could lead to this observed pressure-dependent behavior, and the results support a $\lambda$ that varies in proportion to the pressure applied. Additionally, the compound's electrical resistivity exhibits a change in slope at around 4.5 GPa, and the temperature at which this change occurs is consistent with the onset of superconductivity. Our findings demonstrate that applying hydrostatic pressure can be used to regulate the superconducting properties of flat-band materials.

We investigate the complete recovery of black hole data from the boundary geodesic equations of the Brown-Boyanov-Teitelboim theory, incorporating graviton emission, and examine the implications of this recovery for calculating boundary action correlations. Building on previous work by Jensen et al., we develop a method to recover both the black hole's mass and angular momentum through repeated measurements of two or three boundary data, respectively, and adapt this approach to analyze the recovery of these quantities under the influence of Hawking radiation, effectively incorporating quantum effects into JT gravity.

Deep learning models are often unable to generalize effectively due to overfitting issues, which can be mitigated by incorporating regularization techniques such as data augmentation and noise addition. A novel method presented in this paper involves modifying neural ODE representations to accommodate time-series data with time-varying noise levels. This approach enables models to learn optimal solution trajectories from minimum-cost paths in a combined cost function space, taking into account both a differential equation describing the underlying process and a noise-driven term. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through the use of a neural ODE model trained on a modified version of the Lorenz 96 data set, which features increasing noise levels and initial conditions.

The Transformer architecture has achieved remarkable success in the field of computer vision across various tasks. However, its applications in reinforcement learning, particularly in vision-language tasks, remain limited. This study explores the effectiveness of the Transformer architecture in vision-language tasks, focusing on a novel object recall task. In this task, agents must retrieve an object from memory that matches a language description. To address this challenge, we introduce a state memory module and an object attention module and propose two training approaches. The first approach leverages contrastive learning, while the other utilizes a simulated query language to enhance agent performance. Our Object Recall Transformer (ORT) model outperforms state-of-the-art methods in the benchmark, with its source code and experiments available on GitHub at https://github.com/limlhy/object-recall-transformer.

Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of fine-tuning language models on instruction-based meta learning. Current research has primarily focused on optimizing hyperparameters and improving model architectures for better performance. This paper, however, takes a different approach. It's been found that the performance gap between the source and target tasks in instruction-based meta learning can be attributed to three key factors: the source task's complexity, the similarity between the source and target tasks, and the diversity of tasks available. Building on this understanding, we introduce OPT-IML, a framework that addresses these factors. Specifically, we examine the impact of each factor and develop a novel approach to mitigate their respective limitations. Our results show that OPT-IML significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving substantial gains of 9.1%, 9.3%, and 11.1% in performance. A thorough analysis of our experiments also identifies areas for future research exploration.

The concept of Legitimate Peripheral Participation (LPP) by Wenger enables individuals to engage with a community and acquire knowledge about its domain and social structure, even with minimal time commitment. LPP is characterized by four components: peripheral, peripheral participation, informed participation, and increasing participation. LPP's application extends beyond to include online communities, where it facilitates participation through varying levels of engagement. However, the impact of LPP on online communities and individuals is still a subject of debate, particularly with regards to community involvement and individual learning. This study aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining the Scratch platform, a prominent online community, using a quantitative approach. By analyzing user contributions and engagement over a period of 7.5 years, the study investigates the role of LPP in online communities and community contributors. The findings reveal that many community contributors adhere to LPP principles and contribute to the community's success. Moreover, the LPP framework is found to be essential for informed participation and contributes to the growth of the community. The study's findings contribute to the understanding of online communities and individual learning, and highlight the benefits of LPP for both.

The method of solving many-electron systems using a "transcorrelated" wave function, which incorporates the multibranched exponential form of the Jastrow factor and remaining wave function, has been shown to effectively reduce the complexity of the system. However, the remaining wave function typically cannot provide the same level of accuracy as that achieved with quantum Monte Carlo methods using a Gaussian Jastrow factor. We have developed a new approach to calculate the transcorrelated perturbation theory, which involves transforming the original Hamiltonian to the transcorrelated basis and then constructing the correlation operator. We have applied this method to study the ground state of the uniform electron gas and compared it with the random phase approximation, finding that the transcorrelated perturbation theory significantly improves the results, particularly for electron-electron correlation energies at high densities compared to the random phase approximation.

To enhance the capability of a global solid Earth model to accurately represent variations in deformation rates and to account for the uncertainty associated with observational sites, we introduce a method for physically plausible covariance inflation. We apply this approach to the global solid Earth tomography model EARTHY, which was previously inflated using matrix-based techniques. Our novel method involves two key steps: first, we apply site perturbations to EARTHY to match observed covariance from real-world data, and then we apply a transportation-based inflation scheme to ensure that the resulting covariance meets the physical requirements of the elastic model.
